name: PyTorch
summary: A tensor and neural-network framework that combines imperative tensor computation, tape-based reverse-mode autograd, and dispatch to CPU, accelerator, and extension kernels.

features.name: Imperative tensor runtime
features.description: Tensor operations execute through an imperative API, with tensors living on CPU or GPU devices and operations producing runtime values.
benefits: Supports interactive debugging and data-dependent control flow
Allows a common tensor API across CPU and accelerator devices
costs: Runtime execution can expose more per-operation overhead than ahead-of-time graph execution
Device placement and synchronization remain observable operational concerns

features.name: Tape-based reverse-mode autograd
features.description: Differentiable tensor operations construct a runtime graph of autograd Nodes and gradient edges that can be traversed in reverse during backward execution.
benefits: Handles dynamic computation paths without prebuilding one static graph
Provides hooks and graph metadata for extension and inspection
costs: Retained graph state and saved tensors consume memory
In-place mutation and graph lifetime rules constrain valid programs

features.name: Schema and dispatch-key operator registry
features.description: The dispatcher stores operator schemas and registered kernels, resolves dispatch keys and fallbacks, and exposes registration handles for lifecycle management.
benefits: Separates operator API schemas from backend-specific implementations
Supports Python, composite, autograd, and device-specific extensions
costs: Dispatch-key precedence and fallback rules increase execution-path complexity
Registration and deregistration must preserve dispatcher invariants

features.name: Backend and extension boundary
features.description: The framework integrates CPU and GPU acceleration libraries and exposes C/C++ and Python extension paths around the tensor API.
benefits: Reuses specialized kernels and hardware libraries
Allows custom operators and neural-network layers without replacing the tensor core
costs: Build, binary, and hardware compatibility become part of deployment
Backend-specific behavior can differ in performance and supported operations

mathematical_views.model: Dynamic computation DAG with reverse-mode accumulation
mathematical_views.question: How does a runtime tensor computation record dependencies and propagate gradients from outputs back to differentiable inputs?
assumptions: Each differentiable operation contributes a node and edges to its inputs
The recorded graph is acyclic for one backward traversal
Gradient accumulation is modeled over the framework's tensor value domain

mathematical_views.question: Given an operator and an ordered dispatch-key context, which registered kernel or fallback is selected?
assumptions: Operator schemas and kernel registrations are the observable registry state
Dispatch-key alias inclusion and precedence are fixed for one runtime
A selected kernel preserves the operator schema expected by the caller

mathematical_views.question: Under what conditions can a CPU, accelerator, composite, or extension kernel refine the same operator contract?
assumptions: All implementations are compared against the registered operator schema
Numerical tolerance and device-specific performance are modeled separately from functional behavior
The model does not assume equivalence for unsupported dtypes or edge cases

benefits: Flexible runtime control flow and straightforward debugging
costs: Per-operation runtime behavior and synchronization can limit optimization opportunities

benefits: Dynamic differentiation with local graph construction
costs: Graph retention and saved intermediates increase memory pressure

benefits: One operator surface can select specialized implementations
costs: Dispatch precedence and registration lifecycle are complex global contracts

benefits: Hardware acceleration and extensibility without changing the high-level API
costs: Deployment inherits backend build and compatibility matrices
